notes.front: What is the `GITHUB_TOKEN`, as an administrator sees it?
notes.back: The token granted to workflows; administrators set its default permissions in organisation or repository settings.
notes.explanation: The default can be a restricted set of permissions or a permissive one, so the choice decides how much a workflow can change.
notes.example: Like a visitor’s pass issued to each automated job, whose default access the building manager decides in advance.
notes.evidence: You can choose a restricted set of permissions as the default, or apply permissive settings. You can set the default permissions for the `GITHUB_TOKEN` in the settings for your organization or your repositories.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Setting the permissions of the GITHUB_TOKEN for your organization”

notes.front: What are workflow execution protections?
notes.back: An Actions policy: an allowlist controlling who can trigger GitHub Actions workflows and which events may run them.
notes.explanation: For now they are the only type of Actions policy, and GitHub says it plans to add more over time.
notes.example: Like a guest list at a venue door that names both who may come in and on which nights.
notes.evidence: They currently contain one type of policy: workflow execution protections. GitHub plans to add more policies over time. ## About workflow execution protections With workflow execution protections, you can define an allowlist that controls who can trigger GitHub Actions workflows and which events are permitted to run them.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Actions policies”, “About workflow execution protections”

notes.front: What is a workflow template?
notes.back: A ready-made workflow people can pick when creating a new workflow, so some or all of the writing is done for them.
notes.explanation: It lets everyone in the organisation who may create workflows do so more quickly and easily.
notes.example: Like the company letterhead in a word processor: staff start from it rather than from a blank page.
notes.evidence: Workflow templates allow everyone in your organization who has permission to create workflows to do so more quickly and easily. When people create a new workflow, they can choose a workflow template and some or all of the work of writing the workflow will be done for them.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations”, “Workflow templates”

notes.front: What is a reusable workflow?
notes.back: A workflow that another workflow calls, so the whole workflow is reused instead of being copied and pasted.
notes.explanation: The workflow that uses it is the “caller” and the reusable one is the “called” workflow; one caller can reference several, each in a single line.
notes.example: Like a shared recipe card that several menus point to, rather than each menu rewriting the recipe.
notes.evidence: A workflow that uses another workflow is referred to as a "caller" workflow. The reusable workflow is a "called" workflow. One caller workflow can use multiple called workflows. Each called workflow is referenced in a single line.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations”, “Reusable workflows”

notes.front: If an enterprise enforces no Actions policies, who has full control over GitHub Actions in each organisation?
notes.back: Organisation owners and users with the “Manage organization Actions policies” permission.
notes.explanation: Enterprise policies are what limit the options members have, so without them the decision stays with each organisation.
notes.evidence: Enterprise policies control the options that are available to enterprise members when they use GitHub Actions. If you don't enforce enterprise policies, organization owners and users with the "Manage organization Actions policies" permission have full control over GitHub Actions for their organizations.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise”, “What are policies for GitHub Actions?”

notes.front: An enterprise owner finds that each organisation has chosen its own, different rules on which actions may run. How can the enterprise make one rule apply everywhere?
notes.back: C: enforce it as an enterprise Actions policy.
notes.choices:
A) Ask every organisation to add a CODEOWNERS file to its repositories
B) Nothing is needed: organisations cannot change Actions settings by default
C) Enforce the rule as an enterprise policy under Policies, then Actions
D) Remove the actions from GitHub Marketplace
notes.choicesExplained: CODEOWNERS requests reviewers; it does not govern which actions run. Organisations do control Actions when no enterprise policy is enforced. The enterprise cannot withdraw other people’s actions from GitHub Marketplace.
notes.explanation: Enterprise policies set the options available to members; without one, organisation owners keep full control.
notes.evidence: If you don't enforce enterprise policies, organization owners and users with the "Manage organization Actions policies" permission have full control over GitHub Actions for their organizations.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise”, “What are policies for GitHub Actions?”

notes.front: In the enterprise Actions “Policies” section, which option lets only chosen organisations use GitHub Actions?
notes.back: “Enable GitHub Actions for specific organizations”.
notes.explanation: The other two options switch Actions on for every organisation or off for all of them.
notes.evidence: In the "Policies" section, you can control which organizations within your enterprise can use GitHub Actions, with the following options: * Enable GitHub Actions for all organizations * Enable GitHub Actions for specific organizations * Disable GitHub Actions for all organizations
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise”, “Policies”

notes.front: What stops working in organisations where the enterprise disables GitHub Actions or does not enable it?
notes.back: Code scanning and GitHub Code Quality analysis.
notes.explanation: CodeQL default setup and GitHub Code Quality run as workflows, which need GitHub Actions enabled for the organisation’s repositories.
notes.evidence: GitHub Actions must be enabled for repositories in an organization for the CodeQL code scanning default setup and GitHub Code Quality workflows to run.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise”, “What are policies for GitHub Actions?”

notes.front: An enterprise with 12 organisations wants GitHub Actions in its two platform-team organisations only, while it drafts wider rules. Which enterprise setting fits?
notes.back: D: Enable GitHub Actions for specific organizations.
notes.choices:
A) Enable GitHub Actions for all organizations
B) Disable GitHub Actions for all organizations
C) `Require actions to be pinned to a full-length commit SHA`
D) Enable GitHub Actions for specific organizations
notes.choicesExplained: Enabling for all would include the other ten. Disabling for all would block the two platform teams as well. Commit pinning controls how actions are referenced, not which organisations may use Actions.
notes.explanation: The enablement options choose which organisations may use Actions at all; the other ten would also lose code scanning analysis.
notes.evidence: If you disable GitHub Actions, or do not enable the feature for one or more organizations, this blocks affected organizations from using code scanning and GitHub Code Quality analysis.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise”, “Policies”

notes.front: Which access option lets any action or reusable workflow run, whoever wrote it and wherever it is defined?
notes.back: “Allow all actions and reusable workflows”.
notes.explanation: It sets no limit on author or location, unlike the enterprise-only and select options.
notes.evidence: **Allow all actions and reusable workflows:** Any action or reusable workflow can be used, regardless of who authored it or where it is defined.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise”, “Controlling access to public actions and reusable workflows”

notes.front: Which access option admits only actions and reusable workflows defined in a repository within the enterprise?
notes.back: “Allow enterprise actions and reusable workflows”.
notes.explanation: Being limited to the enterprise’s own repositories, it even blocks actions that GitHub itself wrote.
notes.evidence: **Allow enterprise actions and reusable workflows:** Only actions and reusable workflows defined in a repository within the enterprise can be used. Blocks all access to actions authored by GitHub, such as the `actions/checkout` action.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise”, “Controlling access to public actions and reusable workflows”

notes.front: After an enterprise switches to “Allow enterprise actions and reusable workflows”, every workflow that uses `actions/checkout` fails. What explains it?
notes.back: B: the option blocks GitHub-authored actions such as `actions/checkout`.
notes.choices:
A) The action must now be pinned to a tag
B) That option blocks all actions authored by GitHub, including `actions/checkout`
C) Only reusable workflows are allowed under that option
D) Actions was disabled for the organisations
notes.choicesExplained: No pinning rule is involved, and pinning would require a full commit hash, not a tag. Actions itself is still enabled, since enterprise actions run. The option admits enterprise actions as well as reusable workflows.
notes.explanation: The option admits only what lives in the enterprise’s own repositories; `actions/checkout` lives in GitHub’s `actions` organisation.
notes.evidence: Only actions and reusable workflows defined in a repository within the enterprise can be used. Blocks all access to actions authored by GitHub, such as the `actions/checkout` action.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise”, “Controlling access to public actions and reusable workflows”

notes.front: Which access option allows everything defined in the enterprise plus any actions or reusable workflows matching criteria you specify?
notes.back: “Allow enterprise, and select non-enterprise, actions and reusable workflows”.
notes.explanation: Choosing it opens further settings, such as allowing actions created by GitHub or naming specific actions.
notes.evidence: **Allow enterprise, and select non-enterprise, actions and reusable workflows**: Any action or reusable workflow defined in a repository within the enterprise can be used, plus any action or reusable workflow that matches criteria you specify.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise”, “Controlling access to public actions and reusable workflows”

notes.front: Under the select option, which setting admits every action in the `actions` and `github` organisations?
notes.back: “Allow actions created by GitHub”.
notes.explanation: Those two organisations are where GitHub keeps the actions it authors.
notes.evidence: **Allow actions created by GitHub:** Allows all actions created by GitHub, located in the `actions` and `github` organizations.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise”, “Allow enterprise, and select non-enterprise, actions and reusable workflows”

notes.front: In the allowed-actions list, how do you allow everything except one action, `octo-lab/deploy`?
notes.back: Enter `*, !octo-lab/deploy@*`: `*` allows everything and the `!` prefix blocks the named action.
notes.explanation: By default only what the list names is allowed, so blocking alone would allow nothing else.
notes.evidence: By default, only actions and reusable workflows specified in the list will be allowed. To allow all actions and reusable workflows while also blocking specific actions, use `*, !space-org/action@*`.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise”, “Allow enterprise, and select non-enterprise, actions and reusable workflows”

notes.front: With `Require actions to be pinned to a full-length commit SHA` on, which actions must be pinned?
notes.back: All actions, including the enterprise’s own and those authored by GitHub.
notes.explanation: The rule makes no exception for trusted authors; only reusable workflows keep the option of a tag.
notes.evidence: **Require actions to be pinned to a full-length commit SHA**: All actions must be pinned to a full-length commit SHA to be used. This includes actions from your enterprise and actions authored by GitHub. Reusable workflows can still be referenced by tag.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise”, “Controlling access to public actions and reusable workflows”

notes.front: Commit pinning is required across the enterprise. A workflow calls `octo-lab/ci/.github/workflows/build.yml@v3`. What happens?
notes.back: A: it runs, because reusable workflows may still use a tag.
notes.choices:
A) It runs: reusable workflows can still be referenced by tag
B) It fails: every reference must be a full commit hash
C) It fails unless `v3` is a branch rather than a tag
D) It runs only if an enterprise owner approves the run
notes.choicesExplained: The pinning rule applies to actions, not to reusable workflows. Nothing in the rule favours branches over tags. The rule has no approval step.
notes.explanation: The pinning requirement covers every action, but the docs leave reusable workflows free to use tags.
notes.evidence: This includes actions from your enterprise and actions authored by GitHub. Reusable workflows can still be referenced by tag.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise”, “Controlling access to public actions and reusable workflows”

notes.front: For an enterprise or organisation created on or after {{c1::2 February 2023}}, the `GITHUB_TOKEN` defaults to read-only access for all scopes.
notes.explanation: Older enterprises and organisations keep the earlier default of read and write access for all scopes.
notes.evidence: The default permissions for the `GITHUB_TOKEN` depend on when the enterprise or organization was created: * **Created on or after February 2, 2023** – Defaults to **read-only** access for all scopes. * **Created before February 2, 2023** – Defaults to **read and write** access for all scopes.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise”, “Workflow permissions”

notes.front: One organisation was created in 2021, another in 2024, and neither has changed its workflow permissions. What does the `GITHUB_TOKEN` get by default in each?
notes.back: B: read and write (2021); read-only (2024).
notes.choices:
A) Read-only in both
B) Read and write in the 2021 one; read-only in the 2024 one
C) Read and write in both
D) Read-only in the 2021 one; read and write in the 2024 one
notes.choicesExplained: The default is not the same for both: it depends on the creation date. The reverse pairing swaps the rule: the read-only default applies to the newer organisation.
notes.explanation: The dividing line is 2 February 2023: organisations created before it default to read and write, those after it to read-only.
notes.evidence: **Created on or after February 2, 2023** – Defaults to **read-only** access for all scopes. * **Created before February 2, 2023** – Defaults to **read and write** access for all scopes.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise”, “Workflow permissions”

notes.front: The enterprise has chosen a restrictive `GITHUB_TOKEN` default. Can an organisation owner choose the permissive default?
notes.back: No. A more restrictive enterprise default stops organisations selecting the more permissive one.
notes.explanation: Organisation settings in turn pass a restrictive choice down to their repositories, where the permissive option is disabled.
notes.evidence: the same option is selected in the settings for repositories within your organization, and the permissive option is disabled. If your organization belongs to a GitHub Enterprise account and a more restrictive default has been selected in the enterprise settings, you won't be able to select the more permissive default in your organization settings.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Setting the permissions of the GITHUB_TOKEN for your organization”

notes.front: The default `GITHUB_TOKEN` is read-only, but one workflow needs to write. How can it get more access?
notes.back: Someone with write access edits the `permissions` key in that workflow file.
notes.explanation: The setting is only a default: per-workflow permissions can add or remove access as required.
notes.evidence: Anyone with write access to a repository can modify the permissions granted to the `GITHUB_TOKEN`, adding or removing access as required, by editing the `permissions` key in the workflow file.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Setting the permissions of the GITHUB_TOKEN for your organization”

notes.front: The setting “Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests” is {{c1::disabled}} by default.
notes.explanation: Enabling it is what lets the `GITHUB_TOKEN` create and approve pull requests.
notes.evidence: **Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests** is disabled by default. If you enable this setting, `GITHUB_TOKEN` can create and approve pull requests.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise”, “Workflow permissions”

notes.front: What are two attack patterns that workflow execution protections can disrupt?
notes.back: Two of: poisoned pipeline execution from pull requests; manual-trigger abuse; untrusted-actor execution; misconfiguration exploitation.
notes.explanation: Each maps to a control: restricting `pull_request_target`, limiting `workflow_dispatch`, blocking low-trust identities, or a central policy that overrides a bad workflow file.
notes.evidence: * **Poisoned pipeline execution from pull requests.** Restrict or prohibit `pull_request_target`, including in public repositories where it is most often exploited. * **Manual-trigger abuse.** Limit `workflow_dispatch` so untrusted identities cannot start workflows. * **Untrusted-actor execution.** Block low-trust identities from triggering workflows entirely. * **Misconfiguration exploitation.** Apply central policy that overrides any single misconfigured workflow file.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Actions policies”, “About workflow execution protections”

notes.front: In workflow execution protections, how do actor rules differ from event rules?
notes.back: Actor rules control who can trigger workflows; event rules control which events, such as `push` or `workflow_dispatch`, are permitted.
notes.explanation: By default everyone with write access can trigger workflows, so actor rules let you give a contributor write access without letting them run your pipelines.
notes.evidence: By default, every user with write access to a repository can trigger workflows. Actor rules let you separate who contributes code from who runs your CI, so you can grant a contributor write access without granting them the ability to execute workflows.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Actions policies”, “Available rules”

notes.front: Contractors need write access to push code, but the security team does not want them starting workflows at all. What fits best?
notes.back: B: an actor rule in workflow execution protections.
notes.choices:
A) Lower the contractors to the Triage role
B) An actor rule in workflow execution protections
C) A branch protection rule on the default branch
D) Require approval for fork pull request workflows
notes.choicesExplained: Triage removes the write access the contractors need. A branch protection rule governs merging, not who triggers workflows. Fork approval covers pull requests from forks, not pushes by people with write access.
notes.explanation: Actor rules separate who contributes code from who runs workflows, which is exactly the split asked for.
notes.evidence: Actor rules let you separate who contributes code from who runs your CI, so you can grant a contributor write access without granting them the ability to execute workflows.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Actions policies”, “Available rules”

notes.front: GitHub’s default policy that blocks the `pull_request_target` event in public repositories is enforced from {{c1::2 November 2026}}.
notes.explanation: Public repositories are where `pull_request_target` is most often exploited, so the default policy targets them.
notes.evidence: GitHub has added a default policy that will block the `pull_request_target` event in public repositories. This policy will be enforced on November 2, 2026.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Actions policies”, “About workflow execution protections”

notes.front: Which fork pull request setting requires approval before workflows run for every user who is not an organisation member?
notes.back: “Require approval for all outside collaborators”.
notes.explanation: The two other settings cover first-time contributors only, which is a narrower group.
notes.evidence: **Require approval for all outside collaborators**. Requires approval for all users who are not organization members.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise”, “Fork pull request workflows from outside collaborators”

notes.front: Why can the “first-time contributor” approval settings be sidestepped?
notes.back: Anyone who has had any commit or pull request merged no longer needs approval, so an innocuous typo fix is enough.
notes.explanation: The docs raise this as a warning against relying on the two first-time settings alone.
notes.evidence: When requiring approvals only for first-time contributors (the first two settings), a user that has had any commit or pull request merged into the repository will not require approval. A malicious user could meet this requirement by getting a simple typo or other innocuous change accepted by a maintainer
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise”, “Fork pull request workflows from outside collaborators”

notes.front: By default, the artifacts and log files that workflows generate are kept for {{c1::90}} days.
notes.explanation: The same default covers checks, workflow runs and commit statuses, and administrators can change the period.
notes.evidence: By default, checks, workflow runs, commit statuses, and the artifacts and log files generated by workflows are retained for 90 days. You can change the retention period.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise”, “Check, workflow run, status, artifact and log retention”

notes.front: What retention periods can be set for public repositories and for private and internal repositories?
notes.back: Public: 1 to 90 days. Private and internal: 1 to 400 days.
notes.explanation: From 1 October 2026 the configured period also covers checks, workflow runs and commit statuses, not only artifacts and logs.
notes.evidence: For public repositories, you can configure a period between 1 and 90 days. * For private and internal repositories, you can configure a period between 1 and 400 days. > \[!IMPORTANT] > Starting October 1, 2026, these policies will apply to checks, workflow runs, and commit statuses in addition to artifacts and logs.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise”, “Check, workflow run, status, artifact and log retention”

notes.front: Before anyone changes it, is GitHub Actions enabled for an organisation’s repositories?
notes.back: Yes. By default it is enabled on all repositories and organisations.
notes.explanation: Owners can then disable it, or limit it to the actions and reusable workflows in the organisation.
notes.evidence: By default, GitHub Actions is enabled on all repositories and organizations. You can choose to disable GitHub Actions or limit it to actions and reusable workflows in your organization.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “About GitHub Actions permissions for your organization”

notes.front: An organisation owner opens Settings, then Actions, then General, but cannot change which actions are allowed. What is the likely cause?
notes.back: C: an overriding enterprise policy.
notes.choices:
A) The owner has not enabled two-factor authentication
B) The organisation has no reusable workflows yet
C) The enterprise that manages the organisation has an overriding policy
D) Organisation owners never manage Actions settings
notes.choicesExplained: The docs name no two-factor requirement for these settings. Having no reusable workflows does not lock the policy. Organisation owners do manage these settings when nothing overrides them.
notes.explanation: Enterprise Actions policies take precedence, so an organisation under one may be unable to manage these settings.
notes.evidence: You might not be able to manage these settings if your organization is managed by an enterprise that has overriding policy.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Managing GitHub Actions permissions for your organization”

notes.front: A team keeps a deployment action in a private repository and wants other private repositories in the organisation to use it, without publishing it. What should they do?
notes.back: B: set the repository’s Actions Access to organisation-wide.
notes.choices:
A) Make the repository public and pin the action to a tag
B) In the repository’s Actions settings, set Access to “Accessible from repositories in the organization”
C) Publish the action to GitHub Marketplace as a private listing
D) Copy the action into every repository that needs it
notes.choicesExplained: Making it public is the publishing they want to avoid. Marketplace publishing is public. Copying works but is the duplication the sharing setting avoids.
notes.explanation: An action or reusable workflow can be shared with the organisation from a private repository, without publishing it.
notes.evidence: To grant access to other private repositories in the organization, in the **Access** section at the bottom of the page, select **Accessible from repositories in the 'ORGANIZATION-NAME' organization**.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Sharing actions and workflows with your organization”, “Sharing actions and workflows with your organization”

notes.front: A private repository’s action is shared with the organisation. What can outside collaborators on the other repositories see?
notes.back: The logs of workflow runs that use its actions or workflows, though they have no direct access to it.
notes.explanation: Sharing gives them indirect access to the private repository, which the docs flag as a warning.
notes.evidence: If you make a private repository accessible to GitHub Actions workflows in other repositories, outside collaborators on the other repositories can indirectly access the private repository, even though they do not have direct access to these repositories. The outside collaborators can view logs for workflow runs
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Sharing actions and workflows with your organization”, “Sharing actions and workflows with your organization”

notes.front: Where must an organisation keep its workflow templates?
notes.back: In a `workflow-templates` directory of a repository named `.github` in the organisation.
notes.explanation: Each template sits beside a metadata file that controls how it is shown to people creating a workflow.
notes.evidence: If it doesn't already exist, create a new repository named `.github` in your organization. 2. Create a directory named `workflow-templates`. 3. Create your new workflow file inside the `workflow-templates` directory.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating workflow templates for your organization”, “Creating workflow templates”

notes.front: A template is `ci-node.yml`. What must its metadata file be called, and which two fields must it have?
notes.back: `ci-node.properties.json`, with `name` and `description`.
notes.explanation: Both required fields are displayed in the list of available workflows; icons, categories and file patterns are optional.
notes.evidence: The metadata file must have the same name as the workflow file, but instead of the `.yml` extension, it must be appended with `.properties.json`.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating workflow templates for your organization”, “Creating workflow templates”

notes.front: A template must run on pushes to each repository’s default branch, which is `main` in some repositories and `trunk` in others. What should the template use?
notes.back: D: the `$default-branch` placeholder.
notes.choices:
A) A branch list naming both `main` and `trunk`
B) A separate template for each branch name
C) The `filePatterns` metadata field
D) The `$default-branch` placeholder
notes.choicesExplained: A list of both would run on either branch wherever both exist, and misses any other name. Separate templates duplicate work. `filePatterns` decides where the template is offered, not which branch it targets.
notes.explanation: When a workflow is created from the template, the placeholder is replaced with that repository’s default branch name.
notes.evidence: If you need to refer to a repository's default branch, you can use the `$default-branch` placeholder. When a workflow is created the placeholder will be automatically replaced with the name of the repository's default branch.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating workflow templates for your organization”, “Creating workflow templates”

notes.front: How do reusable workflows and composite actions differ in what they contain?
notes.back: A reusable workflow can contain several jobs; a composite action contains steps only and runs as a single step.
notes.explanation: So a composite action is used inside a job, while a reusable workflow is called directly within a job, not from a step.
notes.evidence: **Workflow jobs** - Composite actions contain a series of steps that are run as a single step within the caller workflow. Unlike reusable workflows, they cannot contain jobs.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations”, “Reusable workflows versus composite actions”

notes.front: Which can use secrets and which can be published to GitHub Marketplace: reusable workflows or composite actions?
notes.back: Reusable workflows can use secrets but cannot be published; composite actions cannot use secrets but can be published.
notes.explanation: The comparison table sets these two differences side by side, so each option has one of the two abilities.
notes.evidence: | Can use secrets | Cannot use secrets | | Cannot be published to the marketplace | Can be published to the marketplace |
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations”, “Key differences between reusable workflows and composite actions”

notes.front: A shared build process has jobs that must run on a different kind of machine from the job that calls them, and each step should appear separately in the logs. Which should the platform team write?
notes.back: A: a reusable workflow.
notes.choices:
A) A reusable workflow
B) A workflow template
C) An action published to GitHub Marketplace
D) A composite action
notes.choicesExplained: A composite action runs as steps inside the caller’s job, on its machine, and logs as one step. A template only gives people a starting file. A published action is a single step, not a set of jobs.
notes.explanation: Jobs in a reusable workflow name their own machine type, and every job and step is logged separately.
notes.evidence: Therefore, if the steps must be run on a type of machine that might be different from the machine chosen for the calling workflow job, then you should use a reusable workflow, not a composite action.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations”, “Reusable workflows versus composite actions”
